values_framework.name: Datadog culture (from careers and engineering pages)

principles.name: Pragmatism and simplicity
principles.description: Solve hard problems the right way with simple, practical solutions. Value simple, fast code over clever designs.
evidence_signals: Chose the simplest design that met the real need and says why
Cut scope or complexity to ship something that worked
Talks about performance and cost, not only features

principles.name: You build it, you own it
principles.description: Teams run what they build. They watch their services, get paged when they break, and fix the cause.
evidence_signals: Was on call for own service and describes a real incident
Added monitoring or alerts so the team knew when something broke
Followed a problem to its root cause and prevented a repeat

principles.name: Honesty and accountability, not blame
principles.description: Be honest about what went wrong. Treat failures as system problems, run postmortems, and own the follow-up.
evidence_signals: Admits own mistake plainly, without blaming others
Describes a postmortem and the system change that came out of it
Gave or received honest feedback and acted on it

principles.name: Humility and a desire to learn
principles.description: Stay low-ego and curious. Learn from colleagues, share what you know, and keep growing.
evidence_signals: Names something they learned from a colleague or a failure
Picked up a new domain or tool quickly for a project
Gives credit to others and is open about gaps

principles.name: Solve tough problems together
principles.description: Work across teams to solve hard problems. Each win is a team win.
evidence_signals: Worked with another team to unblock a shared problem
Helped a teammate or new hire succeed
Uses 'we' for team results and 'I' for own decisions

principles.name: Clear communication and visibility
principles.description: Share clear status, metrics and decisions so others can act, especially during incidents and cross-team work.
evidence_signals: Kept stakeholders or customers updated on a regular cadence
Used metrics or dashboards to make progress visible
Explains a technical point simply to a non-expert

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Past experience, interest in Datadog and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: One or two practical coding problems in a shared editor. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: Two coding rounds below Staff, one at Staff and above. Problems start simple and add constraints. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Often data-heavy systems such as ingestion, time-series storage, alerting or tracing. Used for leveling.

rounds.name: Project deep dive or presentation
rounds.notes: Walk through a system you built: choices, trade-offs, failure modes. At Staff and above this is a presentation to a panel and replaces a coding round.

rounds.name: Behavioral and experience
rounds.interviewer_role: Engineering manager or director of engineering
rounds.notes: Past work, impact, teamwork, ownership and incidents. May include technical questions about past projects.

rounds.name: Team matching
rounds.notes: After a hiring committee approves the loop. Mostly mutual fit: team scope, motivation and what the candidate wants next.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: PM background, interest in Datadog and fit. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: PM screen
rounds.notes: Experience, product sense and approach to PM work. May include a short case.

rounds.name: Product case
rounds.notes: Usually tied to an observability or developer-tools problem in the area of the opening.

rounds.name: Analytical round
rounds.notes: Metrics, success measures and data-driven decisions, for example what a dashboard should show.

rounds.name: Technical round
rounds.notes: Technical understanding of monitoring, cloud and system design at a PM level.

rounds.name: Cross-functional and behavioral
rounds.notes: Working with engineering, shipping, prioritization and failures.

rounds.name: Executive interview
rounds.notes: Only for some roles. Strategy, vision and fit.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background and interest in Datadog. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: Statistics, ML concepts and coding in Python or SQL. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML fundamentals and statistics
rounds.notes: Verbal questions on statistics, modeling and evaluation.

rounds.name: Applied ML design
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior applied scientist or ML engineer
rounds.notes: Design an ML system for observability data, such as anomaly detection on time series, including production monitoring and retraining.

rounds.name: Project presentation or case
rounds.notes: Present a past project or work through an observability ML case.

rounds.name: Behavioral and hiring manager
rounds.notes: Impact of past ML work, models that failed, and explaining results to non-experts.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Sales or solutions engineering role. Background and motivation. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Experience, technical depth and approach to customer engagements.

rounds.name: Panel with sales engineers and account executives
rounds.notes: Customer stories, working with sales and handling a deal or proof of concept that went wrong.

rounds.name: Technical questions
rounds.notes: Cloud, Kubernetes, APM and observability concepts, explained simply for a customer.

rounds.name: Technical demo or presentation
rounds.notes: A prepared demo or technical presentation. Some roles add a take-home. Not simulated in v1.

question_patterns.pattern: A production issue the candidate diagnosed and fixed: how they found the cause, what they did in the moment, and what stopped it happening again
values: You build it, you own it

question_patterns.pattern: A failure or mistake the candidate was part of, how they admitted it, and the system change that followed
values: Humility and a desire to learn

question_patterns.pattern: A project with competing priorities or stakeholders and how the candidate decided what came first
A problem that needed another team's help and how the candidate got it solved without authority over that team
A time the candidate had to learn a new system, language or domain quickly to deliver
values: Humility and a desire to learn

question_patterns.pattern: Walk through the most complex system on the resume: own role, key design choices, and measurable impact
values: You build it, you own it

question_patterns.pattern: Why observability, infrastructure or developer tools, and why this team now
Talk through a design for ingesting, storing and querying high volumes of metrics, logs, events or traces, with throughput and cost trade-offs
Explain why a past system used one technology or design over another, and what the candidate would change now
Take a working design and push it: ten or a hundred times more load, a failed node or region, and how you would know it broke
values: You build it, you own it

question_patterns.pattern: Explain a monitoring concept such as metrics versus logs versus traces, or alert fatigue, clearly to a given audience
Design or improve a feature for engineers who run production systems, with a target user, a success metric and a first version
Define how to measure a product or launch, and what a dashboard for a given leader should show

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a complex production problem you diagnosed and fixed. How did you debug it, and how did you stop it from coming back?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real incident on a system you owned. Explain the first signal (an alert, a customer report), how you narrowed the cause with metrics, logs or traces, and the fix you shipped. Say what you communicated and to whom while it was happening. End with the lasting change: a test, an alert, a runbook or a design change, and how you know it worked. Pitfalls: a story where someone else did the debugging, no root cause, or blaming a person instead of the system.
values: You build it, you own it

looking_for: How you debug a live system step by step
Whether you own the service end to end
strong_signals: Uses metrics, logs or traces to narrow the cause
Names the lasting fix and how it was verified
Kept people informed during the incident
watch_outs: Someone else did the real debugging
No root cause or no prevention step
Blaming a person instead of the system

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you led a project with conflicting priorities. How did you decide what to do first?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the competing asks and who owned each. Show how you made the trade-off visible: impact, cost, deadlines, risk. Explain the decision, who you aligned with, and what you said no to. Give the result and what happened to the deferred work. At senior levels the priorities should cross teams. Pitfalls: doing everything by working late, or a decision with no reasoning.

looking_for: How you weigh competing demands
Whether you align people instead of just choosing
strong_signals: States clear criteria for the trade-off
Says what was dropped and how that was communicated
Shows the outcome
watch_outs: Solving it only by working longer hours

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a major outage or production issue you were part of. What was your role and what changed afterwards?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the impact in plain numbers (users, duration), your exact role in the response, and how the team coordinated. Be honest about what went wrong, including your own part. Describe the postmortem and the system changes it produced, not individual blame. Strong answers mention communication to customers or stakeholders. Pitfalls: a minor bug framed as an outage, or no follow-up.
values: You build it, you own it

looking_for: How you act under incident pressure
Whether you learn at the system level
strong_signals: Clear personal role in the response
A blameless postmortem with concrete changes
Mentions customer or stakeholder updates
watch_outs: A small bug told as a big outage

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a system you built. Why did you choose your main technologies, for example one message queue over another?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give the problem and the constraints first: load, latency, team skills, cost. Explain the main components and the choice under question, with the option you rejected and why. Be honest about what turned out wrong and what you would change now. Show you know the failure modes and how the system was monitored. Pitfalls: listing tools without reasons, or claiming decisions you did not make.

looking_for: Whether your design choices had real reasons
How well you know your own system
strong_signals: Starts from constraints, then the choice
Names the rejected option and why
Admits what you would change
watch_outs: Claiming decisions you did not make

sample_questions.question: How would you design a system that collects, aggregates and shows metrics from thousands of servers in near real time?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale (hosts, points per second, retention) and queries first. Cover an agent that batches and sends data, an ingestion tier behind a queue, aggregation by time window and tags, and a time-series store with compression and rollups. Discuss high-cardinality tags, late data, backpressure and partial failures. Explain the read path and caching for dashboards. Keep it simple first, then scale. Pitfalls: jumping to tools without numbers, or ignoring cost and cardinality.

looking_for: How you size and shape a write-heavy system
Your grasp of time-series trade-offs
strong_signals: Asks about scale and queries first
Handles cardinality, late data and backpressure
Starts simple, then scales

sample_questions.question: Design a service that finds good flight deals from the last week and notifies users when a matching flight appears.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify what a deal is, data sources, freshness and user volume. Sketch ingestion of fare data, storage indexed for the queries you need, a matching step against saved user preferences, and a notification service with de-duplication and rate limits. Discuss batch versus streaming matching, idempotency and what happens when a provider is down. Keep it high level but justify each choice. Pitfalls: skipping requirements, or a design with no failure handling.

looking_for: How you turn a vague product ask into requirements
Clear, justified high-level design
strong_signals: Defines a deal and freshness before designing
Handles duplicate and failed notifications
Compares batch and streaming matching
watch_outs: No thought on failures or duplicates

sample_questions.question: How would you design a distributed tracing system that follows requests across many microservices?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain trace and span ids and how context passes between services. Cover client libraries, a collector, sampling (head versus tail) to control volume, storage keyed by trace id plus indexes for search, and a view that rebuilds the request tree. Discuss overhead on the traced service, clock skew and missing spans. Pitfalls: storing every span with no sampling plan, or ignoring the cost to the application.

looking_for: Understanding of trace context and sampling
Awareness of overhead and volume
strong_signals: Explains context propagation clearly
Compares head and tail sampling
Mentions clock skew or missing spans
watch_outs: Ignoring overhead on the traced service

sample_questions.question: How would you monitor a microservices system that runs on Kubernetes?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the layers: nodes and cluster, pods and containers, services, and the user-facing experience. Name the signals at each layer (resource use, restarts, latency, errors, saturation) and how metrics, logs and traces connect. Explain alerting on symptoms users feel, with fewer noisy alerts, and dashboards per service. Mention tags for ownership and short-lived pods. Pitfalls: a long list of metrics with no alerting strategy.
values: You build it, you own it

looking_for: A layered view of what to monitor
Good alerting judgment
strong_signals: Separates infrastructure and user-facing signals
Alerts on symptoms, not every metric
Links metrics, logs and traces
watch_outs: Listing metrics with no alert plan
Forgetting short-lived pods and ownership tags

sample_questions.question: Design a product that helps engineers reduce alert fatigue.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with who suffers (on-call engineers, team leads) and why: noisy, duplicate or unactionable alerts. Pick one segment and the core problem. Propose a few options such as grouping related alerts, suggesting threshold changes from history, or showing alert quality per team, then choose one first version. Define success, for example fewer pages per on-call shift without more missed incidents. Address the risk of hiding a real problem. Pitfalls: features without a user, or a metric that rewards silencing alerts.

looking_for: Empathy for on-call engineers
A focused first version with a sound metric
strong_signals: Names a clear user and their pain
Picks one option and explains why
A metric that also guards against missed incidents
watch_outs: A feature list with no user
A metric that rewards muting alerts

sample_questions.question: How would you design a product that helps users connect metrics, logs and traces for the same problem?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Frame the user job: going from a symptom to a cause during an incident. Map today's pain, such as switching tools and losing context. Propose a flow that carries shared context (service, time, tags) across the three signals, and pick the first slice to build. Define success, such as time to find the cause or how often users jump between views. Mention data and tagging prerequisites. Pitfalls: a generic all-in-one vision with no first step.

looking_for: Understanding of the incident workflow
Ability to slice a big idea
strong_signals: Starts from the user's job during an incident
Uses shared context to link signals
Picks a first slice and a success metric
watch_outs: Ignoring the data needed to link signals

sample_questions.question: You have three competing feature requests from customers and engineering. How would you decide which to build first?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify each request: who asks, what problem, how many customers, revenue or risk at stake, and effort. Make the criteria explicit and compare the options on them. Look for data, such as usage or support tickets, before deciding. Make a call, say what you will tell the people whose request waits, and how you will revisit it. Pitfalls: a scoring framework with no decision, or going with the loudest customer.

looking_for: Clear prioritization criteria
Willingness to make a call
strong_signals: Asks what problem each request solves
Uses data to compare
Says how the decision is communicated

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a product you launched that did not work. What did you learn?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the goal, the bet you made and how you measured it. Be honest about why it failed and your own part in that. Show what you did next: killed it, changed it, or changed how you validate ideas. Give evidence that the lesson changed later work. Pitfalls: a failure that is really a success, or blaming engineering or timing.
values: Humility and a desire to learn

looking_for: Honesty about your own part
A lesson that changed later work
strong_signals: Had a clear success metric up front
Owns the wrong call
Shows a later decision made differently

sample_questions.question: How would you design a system that detects anomalies in time-series metrics?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the metrics, seasonality, latency needs and the cost of false alarms. Start with a simple baseline (rolling statistics, seasonal decomposition) before a learned model. Discuss labeling, evaluation with precision and recall on past incidents, and per-series versus shared models at scale. Cover running it in production: drift, retraining, and letting users give feedback. Pitfalls: jumping to deep learning with no baseline or no evaluation plan.

looking_for: Practical modeling judgment
A plan to evaluate and run the model
strong_signals: Starts with a simple baseline
Handles seasonality and false alarms
Covers drift and retraining
watch_outs: No way to measure if it works

sample_questions.question: How would you handle concept drift in a model that runs in production?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define drift (input distribution versus the input-label relation). Explain how to detect it: monitor feature distributions, prediction distributions and live accuracy where labels arrive. Describe responses: alerts, scheduled or triggered retraining, and fallbacks. Mention testing a retrained model before it replaces the old one. Pitfalls: retraining blindly on a schedule with no monitoring.
values: You build it, you own it

looking_for: Clear definition of drift types
How you monitor and respond
strong_signals: Monitors inputs, outputs and accuracy
Validates a new model before switching
watch_outs: No monitoring of the live model

sample_questions.question: How would you explain the difference between metrics, logs and traces to a customer, and when each one helps?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give short definitions: metrics are numbers over time, logs are event records, traces follow one request across services. Use one example incident to show how they work together: a metric alerts, a trace shows the slow service, logs show the error. Adjust depth to the audience. Pitfalls: jargon, or treating one signal as enough for everything.

looking_for: Simple, correct explanations
How the signals fit together
strong_signals: One example that uses all three
Adjusts depth to the listener

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a proof of concept with a customer that did not go as planned.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the scene: the customer, success criteria and what was at stake. Explain what went wrong and when you noticed. Show how you were honest with the customer and the account team, what you changed, and the result. End with what you now do differently at the start of a proof of concept. Pitfalls: blaming the customer or the product, or no clear success criteria.

looking_for: Honesty with customers and sales partners
How you recover a deal at risk
strong_signals: Clear success criteria from the start
Raised the problem early
Changed how you run proofs of concept

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-scoped tasks with guidance; loop is mostly coding plus behavioral.
Owns features and the services behind them, including on-call; can talk through a sound design.
Designs and owns systems at high scale, leads projects in the team, and handles incidents end to end. System design strongly affects leveling.
Sets technical direction across teams and explains technical and business reasons for decisions; presents a past project to a panel.
Shapes architecture for a large area of the platform and influences many teams.
Owns a feature area, ships with engineering and measures results.
Owns a product area and its strategy, works across teams, and makes hard prioritization calls.
Leads applied ML projects on observability data from idea to production, and explains results to non-experts.
Runs technical evaluations for enterprise customers on their own, from demo to proof of concept, with account executives.

persona.pace: Moderate; starts with a simple version of a problem, then adds constraints
persona.pushback_style: Asks why each design choice was made, what the candidate did personally, how it scales to much more load, and how they would know it broke
persona.closing_style: Leaves a few minutes for the candidate's questions

case_style.notes: PM cases center on products for engineers who run production systems, such as alerting, logs and traces. Expect metrics and dashboard questions and some technical depth. Market sizing is rarely reported.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: Datadog publishes no formal values list. The six principles are our synthesis of phrases on Datadog's careers pages, a job posting ('pragmatism, honesty, and simplicity'), the incident-response blog post (you build it, you own it; blameless), and employee quotes on Built In. Third-party lists disagree with each other and were not used. values_share is set low at 0.15 because no source reports a separate values round.

loop_structure: the SWE loop agrees across interviewing.io, Codemia and TechPrep, but Datadog's own candidate page gives only generic stages. PM, data_ml and other (sales engineer) loops rest mainly on CleverPrep pages that mix candidate reports with editorial analysis; round names and durations there are approximate.

bar_by_level: SWE titles (Software Engineer I and II, Senior, Staff, Senior Staff, Principal) come from a third-party level list and job titles; internal level codes are not public and are not used. PM, Applied Scientist and Sales Engineer labels are generic job titles, not confirmed Datadog levels. Scope text is our summary.
persona: inferred from prep guides (problems that start simple and add constraints, follow-ups on scaling and design choices) and culture pages; no official description of interviewer style.
scoring_weights: our estimate from emphasized traits in prep guides (ownership, incidents, trade-offs, pragmatism); no public source gives weights.
case_style: based on one prep site's PM page and search snippets of candidate reports; the analytical and dashboard focus is reported but thinly sourced.

sample_questions: all come from third-party prep sites (Codemia, Design Gurus, TechPrep, interviewing.io, CleverPrep), not from Datadog. Design Gurus and CleverPrep pages are partly editorial, so some questions may be typical rather than actually asked.
